narrative:
Based on the assessment, the model estimated a 46% likelihood that you will leave your current position. Since this exceeds the 40% threshold used to determine promotion eligibility, your promotion has been denied. Here is what drove that outcome.

The most influential factor actually worked in your favor: your total years of professional experience, falling in the 1–5 year range, pushed the prediction toward staying. While this may seem counterintuitive, it reflects patterns in the data suggesting employees at this career stage tend to remain in their roles.

However, the second most important factor pushed strongly in the opposite direction. You indicated that you have received other job opportunities while working here. This is notably uncommon — only about 21% of employees who were granted promotions reported the same. The model interprets this as a meaningful signal that you may be considering alternatives, significantly raising the likelihood of departure.

The third factor, working in the medical sector, provided a modest pull toward staying, offering a slight counterbalance to the job opportunities signal.

Ultimately, the presence of outside job offers outweighed the stabilizing factors, tipping the prediction past the threshold.

To improve your chances of being reconsidered, it would help to demonstrate a clear commitment to your current organization. Having an open conversation with your manager about your career development goals and long-term intentions could make a meaningful difference. Showing that you are invested in growing within this organization, rather than exploring outside options, may shift how your situation is evaluated in future promotion cycles.
